description: If your child is hurt at another family's house and a homeowner's insurance policy is in effect, the injury claim will almost certainly be covered.
shortAnswer: If your child sustains an injury while at another family's house and there is a homeowner's insurance policy in effect, your child's injury claim will almost certainly be covered. Don't delay in reporting the injury, however, because all policies have a provision that says if timely notice is not given to the insurance company they can deny coverage.

faq.q: What is Med Pay coverage on a homeowner's insurance policy?
faq.a: “Med Pay” is no-fault coverage, which means it is available to help compensate you for medical expenses related to your child's injury no matter how the injury took place. If you can show that your child was injured on the other family's property, you can recover under the “Med Pay” coverage.

faq.q: What does a bodily injury liability claim pay that Med Pay doesn't?
faq.a: “Med Pay” pays only for your child's medical expenses. A liability claim pays you for medical expenses, any related lost wages, human losses (pain and suffering), and any damages that flow from your child's injury. It pays only when the owner or someone in the owner's family is found to be at fault.

faq.q: Can my child be blamed for their own injury under Georgia's tender years doctrine?
faq.a: It depends on the age of your child. With very young children (4 and under) it is clear that they can't be blamed for hurting themselves. With children older than 6, it is less clear; the issue is one for a jury to decide and is very fact specific.

faq.q: Do I need an attorney for a homeowner's Med Pay claim?
faq.a: Because “Med Pay” claims are no-fault generally you do not need an attorney if that is the only type of claim you plan to bring. If, however, you believe there was fault, it would be worth your while to consult with an attorney.
